ThePharmacist: A henpecked but stoic pharmacist (W.C. Fields) tries to maintains his precarious balance while dealing with demanding customers and his dysfunctional family.

rv: If you listen to the words - it is genuinely funny and even timely and relevant - today. But you have to listen. It is not a sitcom on TV that lasts 22 minutes. It is more for an audience that listens and enjoys good characterizations. An intelligent audience.

Success is not funny. Failure and dysfunctional family situations are the mother’s milk of laughter. W.C. was a comical genius. His pratfalls and constant inability to withstand familial dissent were the basis of his advanced comical critiques. Observe and listen. His quips and sardonic opinions blatantly stated what the constipated Puritans could never bring themselves to confront. That awful elephant in the living room!

Much of Field's humor was based on taking an everyday situation and stretching it to extremes. One example is the gent purchasing a 3 cent stamp from the middle of the sheet and then asking for change for a hundred dollars. Classic Fields. I have to give this less than a highest rating due to poor audio. The video is good though less than perfect.
Some of the gags here remind us of The Blues Brothers -- especially the shoot out. Each vignette is well timed and plays out nicely.
The only problem is most of it is just not that funny.

rv: Georges Méliès was a groundbreaking director who began his career in 1896 (sadly some of his films, especially the early ones, are lost). His innovations were many and deserve your attention if so inclined. This snippet from the Le Papillon fantastique (The Fantastic Ballet) marks another innovation as he begins to use the film making process to manipulate the viewers sense of reality. I have to admit, I like the color. And that is one dead Shelob!

Melies` mastery of the embryonic art of the cinema was truly astounding. As well as the panoply of transformations, disappearances and spatial discontinuities that he archly teased spectators with(to their delight and amazement), we have in this fragment an exmple of the hand painted films that Melies produced. Whole teams of, mainly female, artists painstakingly coloured these movies and what an absolute delight to us cineastes, film historians and film buffs they are. Cracking stuff!

loveLaughsatAndyHardy: Love Laughs at Andy Hardy is a 1946 American comedy film directed by Willis Goldbeck and starring Mickey Rooney, Lewis Stone and Bonita Granville. It was produced by Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. The film is also known under its American promotional title Uncle Andy Hardy. This was the fifteenth and penultimate film in the Andy Hardy series, and the final film featuring Stone as Judge Hardy. The final installment, Andy Hardy Comes Home (1958), was released 12 years later.

rv: I wish all of the Andy Hardy movies could be here on archive.org. This is one of my favorite movie series of all time. The series follows Andy (played by Mickey Rooney) through out his life, from high school all the way to the end of his college career. The entire cast returns for the whole series, reprising their respective roles. In this delightful episode, Andy returns from serving in WWII, completely in love with the idea of marrying his college sweetheart. He re-enters his college life only to find that she has other plans.
The part where they ask him to be the best man and he throws rice at them as they drive off is the most depressing and pathetic scene that has ever been filmed.

This isn't exactly comedy gold, but the cuteness makes it worth seeing.
